target_value.title: U.S. compounding policy (as of 29 October 2026)

entries.value: MOTS-c is not an FDA-approved drug and is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)). MOTS-c was in FDA’s interim Category 2 from 29 September 2023 until 22 April 2026. FDA’s categories list (updated 14 May 2026) does not place it in Category 1, 2 or 3.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (23 July 2026). FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) considered MOTS-c (free base) and MOTS-c acetate for the 503A Bulks List on 23 July 2026. In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither form be included. FDA has not posted minutes or vote results on the meeting page, and this page gives no vote counts. The HHS policy’s Appendix B states that “CDER recommended against listing either form, and the PCAC voted in favor of both forms.” Advisory committee recommendations are non-binding.

Draft interim policy published for comment (announced 28 October 2026). The HHS Office of the Secretary filed a Federal Register notice of availability (FR Doc. 2026-22192; Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496; RIN 0910-ZD94) for a draft “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances”. The notice is scheduled for publication on 30 October 2026, and it states that written comments can be submitted “until 2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register”. OIRA concluded its review on 27 October 2026. MOTS-c is one of six peptides in the policy’s Appendix A. The policy states that, until a peptide “is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list,” HHS “does not intend to take action against a State licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician” compounding with it “when all of the following circumstances are present”.

Scope: the identity listed in Appendix B is MOTS-c acetate, for subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms only. The compounded product may contain only a single active ingredient. This describes the policy’s scope. It is not usage guidance.

Conditions (summary): the bulk substance must come from a facility registered under section 510 with a valid certificate of analysis (COA) whose test results meet the testing standard in Appendix B; the original manufacturer must be FDA-registered and CGMP-compliant, with its location on the certificate; compounders must report products compounded, serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA and to the States, and serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA’s MedWatch program; the label must state “This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale.”; the only co-packaged device may be an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe; and section 503A’s insanitary-conditions and patient-specific prescription requirements still apply.

Not an approval: the notice states that “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed.” The policy makes no safety or efficacy finding for MOTS-c.

Not a Bulks List listing and not Category 1: MOTS-c is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)) and is not in any FDA interim category. The notice says FDA’s future rulemakings “may propose adding some or all of these peptides” to the list; no such proposed rule has been published.

Interim and non-binding: there is no calendar end date. The policy applies until a final rule addresses each peptide, HHS “may revisit” it “if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises”, and the notice says it “is not binding on HHS or the public.”

Research-use-only products: HHS describes the policy as meant to “discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients.” Nothing in the policy treats research-use-only products as covered.

target_value.title: Development Status

entries.value: Retatrutide is not FDA-approved. Phase 3 TRIUMPH results are published, including TRIUMPH-1 (The New England Journal of Medicine, 29 Sep 2026) and TRIUMPH-2 (The Lancet, 29 Sep 2026). Eli Lilly has said it plans to file a U.S. application no later than Q1 2027. On 2 October 2026, FDA concluded on remand that retatrutide is not a biological product and that an application would need to be submitted under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (the drug pathway). A filing plan is not approval. Research-grade retatrutide on PeptideMap is listed for research-use (RUO) comparison only. It is not clinical trial supply, not a prescription, and not medical advice.

target_value.title: Development status (investigational)

entries.value: Retatrutide is an investigational GIP/GLP-1/glucagon receptor agonist. It is not approved by the FDA (or EMA / other regulators cited here) for any indication and is not commercially marketed by Eli Lilly as a prescription medicine. PeptideMap vendor listings are RUO / research-use comparison data only — not trial supply, not expanded-access supply, and not prescriptions.
Company materials continue to describe retatrutide as an investigational molecule that cannot be legally sold or marketed for human use pending approval pathways.

target_value.title: Filing literacy — Lilly’s stated Q1 2027 filing plan (≠ approval)

entries.value: On 23 July 2026, Eli Lilly announced positive topline results from TRIUMPH-2 and TRIUMPH-3 and stated it is completing the comprehensive CMC data package required for a Biologics License Application (BLA) and plans to subsequently submit retatrutide in Q1 2027 for U.S. approval. That sentence is a sponsor filing plan.

Filing is not FDA acceptance (filing decision) and acceptance is not approval. Until FDA receives and files an application and assigns a review clock, there is no agency action date to treat as an approval date.
Do not convert “Q1 2027” into “approved in 2027.” Secondary timeline calendars that project review windows are estimates, not facts, and are not pasted here as predictions.

Later dated statements: Lilly’s 29 September 2026 announcement said it plans to submit a BLA in Q1 2027. On 2 October 2026, FDA concluded on remand that an application for retatrutide would need to be submitted under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Lilly’s 8 October 2026 Seventh Circuit memorandum says it plans to file “no later than the first quarter of 2027” and needs to know which application pathway (biological product or drug) to pursue. See the classification subsection below.

target_value.title: Biologic vs drug classification — FDA decision on remand (2 Oct 2026); Seventh Circuit appeal pending

entries.value: In January 2024, Lilly asked FDA to regulate retatrutide as a biological product under a Biologics License Application (BLA). FDA responded on 18 March 2024 that retatrutide is a drug, not a biological product. Lilly sued in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana (No. 1:24-cv-01503), which sent issues about whether retatrutide is “analogous” to a protein back to FDA. On 2 October 2026, deciding those issues on remand, FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research concluded that “retatrutide is not an analogous product to a protein and is therefore not a biological product. Accordingly, an application for retatrutide would need to be submitted under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.” A redacted copy of the decision was filed in the Seventh Circuit on 8 October 2026 (No. 26-1301, Dkt. 46-2).

Lilly’s appeal in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, Eli Lilly and Company v. Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., No. 26-1301, is from the district court’s judgment. The court heard oral argument on 24 September 2026 and ordered supplemental memoranda on appellate jurisdiction, which both sides filed on 8 October 2026 (Dkt. 45–47). In a footnote, Lilly’s memorandum says FDA’s new decision is “beyond the scope of this appeal” (Dkt. 47, n.3). As of 22 October 2026, no ruling appeared on the docket.

Educational takeaway only: under FDA’s 2 October 2026 decision, an application for retatrutide would be a section 505 drug application. Neither that classification decision nor the pending appeal is an approval decision, and an argument or a pending appeal is not a ruling.

target_value.title: Lilly lawsuits against retatrutide sellers (2026) — separate from the classification case

entries.value: Separately from the 2024 classification case above, Eli Lilly has filed lawsuits in 2026 against businesses it says sell unapproved retatrutide. On 12 August 2026, Lilly announced six suits in federal courts in California and Texas. On 8 October 2026, Bloomberg Law reported five more complaints, filed that day in several federal courts. One of the October complaints, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas (No. 4:26-cv-01294), asserts a single claim of false or misleading advertising under the Lanham Act (15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(B)).

Bloomberg Law reported on 26 October 2026 that Lilly has filed “at least 11 federal lawsuits against a range of online vendors and wellness clinics.” That count is Bloomberg Law’s. PeptideMap has not reviewed every docket.

A complaint states the plaintiff’s allegations; it is not a court finding. PeptideMap has not tracked later rulings, dismissals or settlements in these cases and does not name or characterize the businesses sued.
These suits are private lawsuits, not FDA actions, and they do not decide whether retatrutide is a drug or a biological product. Retatrutide is not FDA-approved.

target_value.title: Access before approval — trials vs expanded access vs grey-market

entries.value: Before any approval, legitimate pathways discussed in primary manufacturer/FDA-process materials are clinical trials and, in limited circumstances, expanded access (sometimes called compassionate use) coordinated with a treating physician and applicable FDA IND / IRB requirements.

Lilly Medical states that retatrutide is not currently FDA-approved; that Lilly is supporting single-patient expanded-access requests for individuals who meet eligibility criteria when they cannot join a trial and have exhausted available options; that availability depends on geography, supply, and case-by-case assessment; and that requests are physician-initiated. ClinicalTrials.gov lists pre-approval expanded access as NCT07629401.

High-level eligibility themes on Lilly Medical include refractory obesity (BMI ≥35 despite highest tolerated approved chronic weight-management therapy), at least two serious or life-threatening obesity-related complications under standard care, and inability to join an ongoing retatrutide (or comparable) trial. This page does not turn those criteria into an application guide or medical advice.
Grey-market / RUO vials sold online are not clinical-trial supply and are not expanded access. Catalog adjacency is not a manufacturer program.

target_value.title: U.S. Senate letter on “research use only” sales (14 October 2026)

entries.value: On 14 October 2026, nine U.S. senators (Jim Banks, Martin Heinrich, Ted Budd, Adam B. Schiff, Tom Cotton, Andy Kim, David H. McCormick, Jon Husted and Todd Young) wrote to Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas about online vendors that sell unapproved drugs and active pharmaceutical ingredients labeled “for research use only.” The letter uses “knockoff retatrutide” as its example and says: “We are concerned that ‘for research use only’ has become a dangerous loophole that undermines the FDA’s authority.” Sen. Banks’s office released the letter on 15 October 2026.

The letter urges FDA “to work more closely with U.S. Customs & Border Protection and other law enforcement agencies to take these illicit drugs off the market and hold the companies selling them accountable,” and requests a briefing on FDA’s enforcement strategy. It cites America’s Poison Centers data showing “a 265% increase in poisonings related to illicit retatrutide in the first four months of 2026 compared to the last four months of 2025.” PeptideMap has not checked that figure against an America’s Poison Centers release.
The letter is a request from members of Congress to FDA. It is not a law, a regulation or an FDA action, and it does not change retatrutide’s status: retatrutide is not FDA-approved.

expected: Phase 2 obesity publications (2023) first put retatrutide on the research radar. TRIUMPH-2 now adds a detailed Phase 3 readout in adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight — factual trial news for encyclopedia/compare context, not prescribing or clinic advice.

Retatrutide is investigational and not approved by the FDA, EMA, or other regulators for any indication. Lilly said on 29 September 2026 that it plans to submit a Biologics License Application (BLA) in Q1 2027. On 2 October 2026, in a decision on remand from a federal district court, FDA concluded that retatrutide is not a biological product and that an application for it would need to be submitted under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (the drug pathway). Lilly’s related appeal in the Seventh Circuit (No. 26-1301) had no ruling as of 22 October 2026. A filing plan is not marketing authorization. PeptideMap is not a pharmacy or clinic. Vendor listings are RUO / research-use comparison data only — not prescriptions, not compounding advice, not clinical-trial supply, and not expanded-access supply. Products sold online under this name are not Lilly trial supply. Reports of deaths and adverse effects linked to products sold as retatrutide (October 2026) are unverified and do not establish causation.

entries.value: The Phase 2 trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2023, showed retatrutide achieved up to 24.2% body weight reduction at 48 weeks at the highest dose — exceeding all previous results from any single pharmacological agent.\n\nThe compound was generally well-tolerated, with nausea, diarrhea, and vomiting as the most common adverse events (consistent with GLP-1-class effects). Phase 3 TRIUMPH results have since been published; see the TRIUMPH-1 and TRIUMPH-2 subsections. Publication is not FDA approval, and those figures are not a dose.

TRIUMPH-2 (NCT05929079) was a registrational Phase 3 trial: 1,152 adults with type 2 diabetes and BMI ≥27 kg/m² were randomized to once-weekly retatrutide trial arms (4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg) or placebo for 80 weeks (EASD 2026 presentation; simultaneous Lancet publication, 29 Sep 2026). Figures below describe what was reported in that study — not how anyone should use research materials sold as RUO.

Efficacy estimand (Lilly press release, 29 Sep 2026) — models remaining on assigned intervention without prohibited weight-management treatments:

• 4 mg: mean weight change −12.7% (−29.8 lbs); A1C −1.4
• 9 mg: mean weight change −19.1% (−45.4 lbs); A1C −1.6
• 12 mg: mean weight change −20.8% (−49.6 lbs); A1C −1.5
• Placebo: mean weight change −4.0% (−9.3 lbs); A1C −0.2

Baseline averages cited by Lilly: weight ~106.4 kg, BMI ~38.2 kg/m², A1C ~7.7%. At 12 mg, Lilly reported 52.0% of participants achieving ≥20% weight reduction and 34.9% achieving ≥25% (efficacy estimand); 59.5% no longer met BMI criteria for obesity. Among participants with baseline BMI ≥35, mean loss at 12 mg was reported as 23.4% (60.8 lbs). Up to 40.0% reached A1C <5.7% (not family-wise type I error controlled per Lilly footnote).

Treatment-regimen estimand (Lancet abstract Findings): mean percent weight change −11.9% (4 mg), −16.8% (9 mg), and −18.8% (12 mg) versus −5.1% placebo (estimated treatment differences vs placebo −6.9%, −11.8%, −13.8%; p<0.0001 for all). Prefer stating which estimand you quote; do not mix them in one sentence without labeling.

Safety (Lilly): most common AEs vs placebo included diarrhea (27.4% / 33.5% / 33.6% vs 13.2%), nausea (13.7% / 20.8% / 28.0% vs 8.0%), constipation (14.0% / 16.2% / 16.8% vs 9.4%), decreased appetite (5.8% / 12.3% / 17.1% vs 4.5%), vomiting (5.5% / 10.2% / 15.7% vs 4.2%). Dysesthesia 4.5% / 5.6% / 7.3% vs 0.7%. Discontinuations due to AEs: 3.8% / 11.6% / 7.7% vs 4.9% placebo. Highest-dose CV risk-factor changes reported by Lilly included average reductions of 39.5% triglycerides, 19.6% non-HDL cholesterol, 10.8 mmHg systolic BP, 6.7 in (16.9 cm) waist circumference, and 58.3% hsCRP — risk factors, not CV outcomes from this trial.

entries.value: TRIUMPH-1 (NCT05929066) is not TRIUMPH-2. Jastreboff and colleagues, for the TRIUMPH-1 Investigators, reported it in The New England Journal of Medicine (29 Sep 2026; DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2604169; PMID 42814954): adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes, randomized to once-weekly retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg or placebo for 80 weeks (2,339 participants). The abstract states that, for weight-related endpoints, intercurrent events were handled by a treatment-regimen estimand. Under that analysis, mean percent change in body weight was −17.6% (4 mg), −23.7% (9 mg), and −25.0% (12 mg) versus −3.9% with placebo. Those abstract figures are the treatment-regimen result. They are not a treatment recommendation and not a head-to-head comparison with semaglutide, tirzepatide, or eloralintide. The same paper’s abstract does not print −28.3%. Lilly Medical’s table of TRIUMPH-1 outcomes, which cites that NEJM article, lists a separate efficacy estimand: percent change in body weight at 80 weeks was −19.0% (4 mg), −25.9% (9 mg), and −28.3% (12 mg) versus −2.2% with placebo. −28.3% is not the abstract primary weight result. TRIUMPH-2 remains the separate type 2 diabetes plus obesity or overweight trial; its published figures are not restated here and are not a ranking against TRIUMPH-1. PeptideMap is a research-use (RUO) comparison publisher, not a clinic or pharmacy. This is not medical advice and not a dose.

expected.title: TRIUMPH-3 topline (Lilly, 23 Jul 2026) — not a peer-reviewed cardiovascular-outcomes paper

entries.value: No. TRIUMPH-3 (NCT05882045) is not sourced from a peer-reviewed NEJM or Lancet cardiovascular-outcomes paper. Eli Lilly’s 23 July 2026 topline is the source. The trial enrolled adults with severe obesity (BMI ≥35 kg/m²) and established cardiovascular disease, with or without type 2 diabetes (1,949 participants; 9 mg, 12 mg, or placebo; 80 weeks). Under the efficacy estimand in that release, mean percent weight change at 80 weeks was −21.6% (9 mg) and −22.6% (12 mg) versus −3.2% with placebo. That is not the TRIUMPH-1 or TRIUMPH-2 result, and a treatment-regimen weight figure for TRIUMPH-3 was not in the release. The same release reported pre-specified in-study analyses of time to first event for pooled 9 mg and 12 mg versus placebo. MACE-5 was 44 events versus 52 (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.22). MACE-3 was 27 events versus 23 (hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.96). Both intervals include 1. The release does not establish a reduction in cardiovascular events. It says these events occurred less frequently than anticipated in both the retatrutide and placebo arms. Urinary tract infection in that topline was 6.1% (9 mg) and 7.0% (12 mg) versus 5.3% with placebo in TRIUMPH-3. This is not medical advice and not a dose.
The TRIUMPH Phase 3 program evaluates retatrutide across related obesity and complication settings. Names below are literacy labels only. Prefer the estimand label printed in the source you cite.

TRIUMPH-1 (NCT05929066) — adults with obesity without diabetes; NEJM 29 Sep 2026 (DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2604169; PMID 42814954). Abstract weight result uses a treatment-regimen (ITT) estimand: mean percent body-weight change −17.6% (4 mg), −23.7% (9 mg), −25.0% (12 mg) versus −3.9% placebo. A separate efficacy-estimand row of −28.3% at 12 mg (vs −2.2% placebo) appears on Lilly Medical’s TRIUMPH-1 outcomes table citing that paper — keep −25.0% and −28.3% labeled separately; do not present −28.3% as the abstract’s treatment-regimen primary weight line.

TRIUMPH-2 (NCT05929079) — adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight; EASD / Lancet 29 Sep 2026 (DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(26)01861-1). Do not rewrite live figures. Locked efficacy estimand includes up to −20.8% mean weight change at 12 mg vs −4.0% placebo; locked treatment-regimen includes −18.8% at 12 mg vs −5.1% placebo.

TRIUMPH-3 (NCT05882045) — adults with severe obesity (BMI ≥35) and established cardiovascular disease, with or without T2D; Lilly topline 23 Jul 2026 (not treated here as a peer-reviewed cardiovascular-outcomes paper). Efficacy-estimand mean weight change −21.6% (9 mg) and −22.6% (12 mg) versus −3.2% placebo. Pre-specified in-study MACE-5 HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.55–1.22) and MACE-3 HR 1.12 (95% CI 0.64–1.96); intervals include 1 — the release does not establish cardiovascular-event reduction.

Label topline versus peer-reviewed whenever you quote. July 2026 PR Newswire is topline for TRIUMPH-2/3 efficacy-estimand headlines; September 2026 Lancet is peer-reviewed for TRIUMPH-2 treatment-regimen Findings; September 2026 NEJM is peer-reviewed for TRIUMPH-1 treatment-regimen weight means.

expected.title: Obstructive sleep apnea trials (NEJM, 20 Oct 2026) — developer-affiliated (Lilly-funded)

entries.value: On 20 October 2026, The New England Journal of Medicine published online the TRIUMPH-1-OSA and TRIUMPH-2-OSA results (full title under References) by Grunstein RR, Somers VK, Azarbarzin A, Malhotra A, Sands SA, Lucey BP, Allen SE, Giblin K, Falcon BL, Park SY, Lou J and Krueger K, for the TRIUMPH-1-OSA and TRIUMPH-2-OSA Investigators (DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2611477; PMID 42904878). Developer-affiliated: the abstract states the work was funded by Eli Lilly, the company developing retatrutide.

Design (from the abstract): two phase 3, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials nested within the larger TRIUMPH-1 (NCT05929066) and TRIUMPH-2 (NCT05929079) basket trials. They enrolled adults with moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and a body-mass index of at least 27, without type 2 diabetes (TRIUMPH-1-OSA, 243 randomized) or with type 2 diabetes (TRIUMPH-2-OSA, 448 randomized). Participants were assigned to one of three retatrutide dose arms or placebo. Baseline mean apnea–hypopnea index (AHI) was 58.6 and 55.9 events per hour, and baseline mean body weight was 119.6 and 115.9 kg.

Primary end point: change in AHI (the average number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep) at 80 weeks in the middle and highest dose arms, analyzed with a hybrid-treatment estimand. Mean AHI changes at 80 weeks in TRIUMPH-1-OSA were −22.9 (lowest dose arm), −34.3 (middle) and −31.7 (highest) events per hour versus −9.9 with placebo (differences vs placebo −13.0 [95% CI −23.0 to −3.0], −24.4 [95% CI −34.1 to −14.7] and −21.9 [95% CI −32.2 to −11.5]). In TRIUMPH-2-OSA they were −19.2, −24.7 and −25.4 versus −10.3 with placebo (differences −8.9 [95% CI −15.9 to −2.0], −14.4 [95% CI −21.6 to −7.2] and −15.1 [95% CI −22.5 to −7.7]).

Intention-to-treat (ITT) estimand, differences from placebo in the same arm order: TRIUMPH-1-OSA −13.2 (95% CI −22.6 to −3.9), −24.7 (95% CI −34.1 to −15.3) and −22.5 (95% CI −31.9 to −13.1); TRIUMPH-2-OSA −8.8 (95% CI −15.8 to −1.7), −13.9 (95% CI −21.3 to −6.6) and −15.0 (95% CI −22.5 to −7.4). Label which estimand you quote.

Key secondary end point (treatment-regimen estimand): mean percent change in body weight across the retatrutide arms was −12.5% to −22.2% in TRIUMPH-1-OSA and −12.1% to −18.5% in TRIUMPH-2-OSA, versus −4.8% and −5.6% with placebo.

Safety, as summarized in the abstract: the most common adverse events were gastrointestinal. The abstract concludes that retatrutide produced significantly greater decreases in AHI than placebo in these trial populations.

Literacy note: these are results from supervised clinical trials in a defined population. Retatrutide is investigational and not approved for obstructive sleep apnea or any other indication. The results do not describe products sold online as retatrutide and are not guidance for use.

TRIUMPH-2 compared retatrutide with placebo, not with semaglutide or tirzepatide. Do not present TRIUMPH-2 percentages as a three-way ranking. Mechanistically, retatrutide adds glucagon receptor agonism to GIP/GLP-1 activity, whereas semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist and tirzepatide is a dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist — different trials, populations, and endpoints. A dedicated Phase 3 comparison versus tirzepatide (TRIUMPH-5, NCT06662383) is registered separately; do not invent results. Older Phase 2 obesity data (e.g., Jastreboff et al., NEJM 2023) remain useful background for non-diabetes obesity cohorts but are not interchangeable with TRIUMPH-2’s diabetes population.

expected.title: Reported safety signals outside clinical trials (as of 22 October 2026)

entries.value: This section summarizes reports about products sold under the name retatrutide outside Lilly's clinical trials. It is separate from the TRIUMPH clinical-trial results and does not change them. None of the reports below establishes that retatrutide caused any event. In most cases, the identity, content, and purity of the product involved are unknown. Products sold online under this name are not Lilly trial supply.

FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) death reports, as reported by CBS News. On 13 October 2026, CBS News reported that FDA had received two reports of deaths after people took products claiming to be retatrutide. CBS said it reviewed redacted FAERS reports obtained under the Freedom of Information Act. According to CBS, the first report (July 2026) described a 41-year-old woman who had cardiac arrest; the report listed retatrutide as a "suspect product" obtained "from an unreliable source." The second report (September 2026) described a 49-year-old patient who had severe dehydration, malnutrition, and cardiac arrest after buying the product from an online peptide vendor. CBS reported that it could not independently verify the reports, that FDA declined to say whether it had verified them, and that neither death was connected to a clinical trial. CBS also reported Lilly's statement that the reports "make clear the two individuals were taking black-market retatrutide." PeptideMap has not seen these reports. The public openFDA FAERS data (last updated 30 July 2026) listed 44 reports in which retatrutide appears as a drug name and no report coded as a death. That dataset predates the September report and may not yet include the July report.

Poison center exposures, as reported by CBS News. CBS reported that America's Poison Centers logged 862 retatrutide exposures in the three months ending in September 2026, 460 in the three months before that, and 249 in the first three months of 2026. America's Poison Centers began tracking retatrutide in late 2025. CBS noted that rising counts are common for a newly monitored drug. An exposure call is not a confirmed adverse effect. PeptideMap has not checked these figures against a public America's Poison Centers or NPDS release.

Limits of FAERS. FAERS is a spontaneous reporting system. Reports are not verified by FDA, can be incomplete or duplicated, and do not show that a product caused an event. For grey-market or "research use" products, the substance actually taken is usually unknown. Report counts cannot be used to estimate how often an event happens.

Social-media pharmacovigilance study (JAMA Network Open, published online 14 October 2026; PMID 42873503). Sehgal NKR, Tronieri JS, Rader B, Ungar L, and Guntuku SC published "Self-Reported Adverse Effects Among Social Media Users Taking Nonapproved Retatrutide" in JAMA Network Open (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.38929). The study was a cross-sectional analysis of 148,640 retatrutide-related Reddit posts and comments. These came from 38,936 users across 27 communities, posted between May 2021 and December 2025. Large language models classified self-reported use and mapped the symptoms users attributed to retatrutide to MedDRA Preferred Terms, and the authors manually validated 100 posts. The models identified 13,589 users reporting current use. Of these, 7,823 had at least one mapped term after prespecified weight-loss and appetite-suppression terms were excluded. Among those 7,823 users, the most frequent terms were increased appetite (17.1%), fatigue (15.2%), increased energy (12.4%), nausea (11.6%), food craving (7.3%), insomnia (6.1%), and heart rate increased (4.8%). The authors note that gastrointestinal symptoms were common but not dominant, which differs from phase 2 trial findings.

Limits the authors themselves state: the findings are hypothesis-generating. Product identity, purity, dose, route, duration, concomitant medications, and medical history cannot be verified. Reddit users may not represent all users, and adverse events may be preferentially reported. The analysis cannot assess incidence, causality, dose-response, or comparative safety. The reported events may also reflect reconstitution practices, and natural language processing and MedDRA mapping may miss or misclassify symptoms. The reports may reflect product variability, peptide stacking, user characteristics, or misattribution. The study's comparison with semaglutide and tirzepatide was descriptive only, with unmatched samples and no statistical tests.
These reports describe unregulated products and cannot be compared directly with the controlled TRIUMPH trial safety data.

entries.value: Tesamorelin (Egrifta) is FDA-approved for reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected patients with lipodystrophy. Phase III trials (n=816) demonstrated a mean reduction of 15-18% in visceral adipose tissue (VAT) measured by CT scan after 26 weeks, compared to increases in placebo groups. Trunk fat reduction was accompanied by improvements in patient-reported body image.
The VAT reduction was specific — subcutaneous fat was not significantly affected. Upon discontinuation, VAT returned toward baseline, indicating the need for continuous treatment to maintain effect.

The TERALYTICS trial evaluated tesamorelin for hepatic steatosis in HIV patients. Results showed a 37% relative reduction in hepatic fat fraction (by MRI-PDFF) vs 10% with placebo. A significant proportion of patients achieved resolution of NAFLD. This has generated interest in tesamorelin for NASH treatment in broader populations.

A 20-week RCT in healthy older adults (n=152) demonstrated that tesamorelin improved executive function and verbal memory compared to placebo. Adults with higher baseline VAT showed the greatest cognitive improvements, suggesting a link between metabolic and cognitive benefits. Larger trials are ongoing to evaluate tesamorelin for mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease prevention.

entries.value: Intravenous NAD+ is offered in some clinical settings, including addiction medicine, but controlled human evidence is limited. A small human pilot study (Front Aging Neurosci 2019) found that, during an intravenous infusion, NAD+ was rapidly and completely removed from plasma for at least the first 2 hours, with a metabolite profile consistent with breakdown by NAD+-consuming enzymes; urinary products included NAD+ itself and methylnicotinamide. Multiple clinical trials have evaluated oral NMN and NR supplementation. In a 10-week randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial in postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were overweight or obese, NMN increased muscle insulin sensitivity (measured with a hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp), muscle insulin signaling and the expression of muscle-remodeling genes (Science 2021). Whole-blood NAD+ changes with NR supplementation (Nat Metab 2026). A 2025 review concluded that, overall, human trials of NAD+ precursors have shown limited efficacy (Nat Metab 2025).\n\nThe key question — whether raising NAD+ in humans produces the benefits reported in mice — remains under active investigation.

target_value.title: U.S. regulatory status — compounding policy (as of 29 October 2026)

entries.value: BPC-157 is not an FDA-approved drug and is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)). In 2026 two separate U.S. steps concerned BPC-157 and pharmacy compounding: a non-binding advisory committee vote in July and a draft interim enforcement-discretion policy that the HHS Office of the Secretary published for comment in October. Neither one approves BPC-157 or places it on the 503A Bulks List. BPC-157 was in FDA’s interim Category 2 from September 2023 until 22 April 2026. FDA’s categories list (updated 14 May 2026) does not place it in Category 1, 2 or 3.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (23 July 2026). FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) considered BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate for the 503A Bulks List on 23 July 2026. In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither form be included. FDA has not posted minutes or vote results on the meeting page, and this page gives no vote counts. The HHS policy’s Appendix B states that “Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) recommended against listing either form, and the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) voted in favor of inclusion.” Advisory committee recommendations are non-binding.

Draft interim policy published for comment (announced 28 October 2026). The HHS Office of the Secretary filed a Federal Register notice of availability (FR Doc. 2026-22192; Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496; RIN 0910-ZD94) for a draft “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances”. The notice is scheduled for publication on 30 October 2026, and it states that written comments can be submitted “until 2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register”. OIRA concluded its review on 27 October 2026. BPC-157 is one of six peptides in the policy’s Appendix A. The policy states that, until a peptide “is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list,” HHS “does not intend to take action against a State licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician” compounding with it “when all of the following circumstances are present”.

Scope: the identity listed in Appendix B is BPC-157 acetate only, for “subcutaneous, intramuscular, oral, and topical dosage forms”, with the amino acid sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val. Other forms, including BPC-157 free base, are outside the listed identity. The compounded product may contain only a single active ingredient, so blends are outside the policy. For oral forms the compounder is expected to keep documentation of adequate oral bioavailability in humans. This describes the policy’s scope. It is not usage guidance.

Conditions (summary): the bulk substance must come from a facility registered under section 510 with a valid certificate of analysis (COA) whose test results meet the testing standard in Appendix B; the original manufacturer must be FDA-registered and CGMP-compliant, with its location on the certificate; compounders must report products compounded, serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA and to the States, and serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA’s MedWatch program; the label must state “This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale.”; the only co-packaged device may be an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe; and section 503A’s insanitary-conditions and patient-specific prescription requirements still apply.

Not an approval: the notice states that “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed.” The policy makes no safety or efficacy finding for BPC-157.

Not a Bulks List listing and not Category 1: BPC-157 is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)) and is not in any FDA interim category. The notice says FDA’s future rulemakings “may propose adding some or all of these peptides” to the list; no such proposed rule has been published.

Interim and non-binding: there is no calendar end date. The policy applies until a final rule addresses each peptide, HHS “may revisit” it “if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises”, and the notice says it “is not binding on HHS or the public.”

Research-use-only products: HHS describes the policy as meant to “discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients.” Nothing in the policy treats research-use-only products as covered.

entries.value: One attractive feature of BPC-157 in research is its apparently favorable safety profile in animals. Toxicology studies have found no lethal dose even at extremely high amounts:

target_value.title: Theoretical Concerns

entries.value:
The most prominent theoretical concern is BPC-157's ability to promote growth factors and blood vessel formation. While beneficial for healing injuries, this raises a question: could BPC-157 unintentionally help existing cancer cells grow or spread? Cancerous tumors often exploit the same pathways (like FAK/paxillin and VEGF) to invade tissues and nourish themselves with blood supply.

This idea is currently theoretical – no study has shown BPC-157 causes cancer in animals or humans. In fact, one lab test showed BPC-157 inhibited growth of a particular cancer cell line in culture. Nonetheless, experts urge caution until more is known about long-term effects.

entries.value: BPC-157 is not an FDA-approved drug and is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)). In 2026 two separate U.S. steps concerned BPC-157 and pharmacy compounding: a non-binding advisory committee vote in July and a draft interim enforcement-discretion policy that the HHS Office of the Secretary published for comment in October. Neither one approves BPC-157 or places it on the 503A Bulks List. BPC-157 was in FDA’s interim Category 2 from September 2023 until 22 April 2026. FDA’s categories list (updated 14 May 2026) does not place it in Category 1, 2 or 3.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (23 July 2026). FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) considered BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate for the 503A Bulks List on 23 July 2026. In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither form be included. FDA has not posted minutes or vote results on the meeting page, and this page gives no vote counts. The HHS policy’s Appendix B states that “Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) recommended against listing either form, and the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) voted in favor of inclusion.” Advisory committee recommendations are non-binding.

Draft interim policy published for comment (announced 28 October 2026). The HHS Office of the Secretary filed a Federal Register notice of availability (FR Doc. 2026-22192; Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496; RIN 0910-ZD94) for a draft “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances”. The notice is scheduled for publication on 30 October 2026, and it states that written comments can be submitted “until 2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register”. OIRA concluded its review on 27 October 2026. BPC-157 is one of six peptides in the policy’s Appendix A. The policy states that, until a peptide “is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list,” HHS “does not intend to take action against a State licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician” compounding with it “when all of the following circumstances are present”.

Scope: the identity listed in Appendix B is BPC-157 acetate only, for “subcutaneous, intramuscular, oral, and topical dosage forms”, with the amino acid sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val. Other forms, including BPC-157 free base, are outside the listed identity. The compounded product may contain only a single active ingredient, so blends are outside the policy. For oral forms the compounder is expected to keep documentation of adequate oral bioavailability in humans. This describes the policy’s scope. It is not usage guidance.

Conditions (summary): the bulk substance must come from a facility registered under section 510 with a valid certificate of analysis (COA) whose test results meet the testing standard in Appendix B; the original manufacturer must be FDA-registered and CGMP-compliant, with its location on the certificate; compounders must report products compounded, serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA and to the States, and serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA’s MedWatch program; the label must state “This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale.”; the only co-packaged device may be an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe; and section 503A’s insanitary-conditions and patient-specific prescription requirements still apply.

Not an approval: the notice states that “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed.” The policy makes no safety or efficacy finding for BPC-157.

Not a Bulks List listing and not Category 1: BPC-157 is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)) and is not in any FDA interim category. The notice says FDA’s future rulemakings “may propose adding some or all of these peptides” to the list; no such proposed rule has been published.

Interim and non-binding: there is no calendar end date. The policy applies until a final rule addresses each peptide, HHS “may revisit” it “if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises”, and the notice says it “is not binding on HHS or the public.”

Research-use-only products: HHS describes the policy as meant to “discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients.” Nothing in the policy treats research-use-only products as covered.

It's important to emphasize: there are no large-scale, definitive clinical trials of BPC-157 in humans yet, and any use outside of research is considered off-label and unapproved.

"Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence" when it comes to safety. Because BPC-157 has not been extensively studied in people, there could be side effects that haven't been observed in small samples. Minor side effects like headaches, dizziness, or injection site reactions might not show up in tiny studies but could in larger populations.

Regulatory status (as of 29 October 2026): BPC-157 is not approved by FDA and is not on the 503A Bulks List. A July 2026 advisory committee vote is non-binding. A draft interim enforcement-discretion policy published for comment by the HHS Office of the Secretary (FR Doc. 2026-22192) describes when HHS does not intend to take action against 503A compounding of BPC-157 acetate. It is not an approval, has no fixed end date, may be revisited by HHS, and makes no safety or efficacy finding. PeptideMap does not predict outcomes.

entries.value:
To date, only minimal human testing has been published. A 2025 pilot study (Lee and Burgess, Alternative Therapies in Health and Medicine; PMID 40131143), carried out at a private clinic in Florida, gave BPC-157 by intravenous infusion on two consecutive days to two adults who had received intravenous BPC-157 before. The authors reported no side effects and no measurable changes in the tested heart, liver, kidney, thyroid and blood glucose markers.

With two participants, no control group and three days of follow-up, the study cannot establish safety. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document for its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee notes that the published human studies of BPC-157 were of short duration, had small sample sizes and gave limited information on safety.

entries.value: A Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers, PCO-02 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02637284, sponsor PharmaCotherapia), was registered in December 2015 to assess the safety and pharmacokinetics of BPC-157 oral tablets against placebo, with a single-administration part and a two-week repeated-administration part and an estimated enrollment of 42. The registry record was last updated in December 2015, its status is listed as unknown, and no results are posted. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document states that FDA was unable to find an associated published study.

Published human data on BPC-157 are limited to a few small, short studies. Most had no control group; the two placebo-controlled studies FDA identified (rectal enemas in healthy volunteers and in people with ulcerative colitis) are available only as meeting abstracts. A 2026 systematic review (Poolton et al., Acta Orthopaedica Belgica; PMID 42885452) rated the overall certainty of evidence as very low. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document concluded that there is insufficient clinical safety information to characterize the safety profile of BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate. Until controlled human trials are published, any human use is experimental.

Clinical studies supporting approval showed significant improvements in anxiety scores compared to placebo, with onset of action within 1-3 days.\n\nImportantly, no sedation, cognitive impairment, or dependence was observed — addressing the major limitations of benzodiazepine therapy.
